steps.body:
A derivative is a **limit**, and limits can fail.

At a corner, the slope coming from the left and the slope coming from the right disagree. Two different answers means the limit does not exist — so f′ does not exist there, however smooth the curve looks elsewhere.
Drag across the corner and watch f′ break.

widget.prompt: f(x) = |x|. Drag x to the one place where the derivative does NOT exist.
widget.successFeedback: x = 0. Look at what f′ did underneath: it sat at −1 all the way in from the left, jumped to +1 on the right, and left a HOLE at 0. Both one-sided slopes exist and they disagree — and a limit with two answers has no answer. The curve is perfectly continuous there; continuity was never enough.
widget.lowFeedback: Not there yet — the tangent still fits perfectly, sloping down at −1. Keep sliding right.
widget.highFeedback: Past it — the tangent fits again, now sloping up at +1. Come back to the corner.

cml.actionGoal: Move along a function and coordinate position, local slope, and derivative graph.

predict.prompt: f(x) = |x| has no derivative at x = 0. The reason is that…

options.label: The function is not defined there
The slope from the left and the slope from the right disagree

predict.reveal: They disagree — −1 from the left, +1 from the right — and a limit that returns two answers returns none. |x| is perfectly defined and perfectly continuous at 0. Differentiability is the stronger promise, and this is exactly where it fails while continuity survives.

explanationVariants: |x| is continuous at 0 — you can draw it without lifting the pen — but the left slope is −1 and the right slope is +1, so the limit defining f′(0) does not exist.
Differentiability implies continuity. The converse is false, and |x| is the counterexample.

widget.prompt: |x| is continuous at x = 0 but has no derivative there. What does that tell you?

options.label: Continuity is necessary for differentiability, but not sufficient.
options.feedback: Right, and the implication runs one way only: differentiable ⇒ continuous, never the reverse.

options.label: Continuity and differentiability are the same thing.
options.feedback: |x| is the standing refutation: continuous everywhere, differentiable everywhere except one point.

options.label: |x| must be discontinuous at 0.
options.feedback: It is not — the two halves meet at (0, 0) with no gap and no jump. The failure is in the SLOPE, not the value.

options.label: The derivative is 0 at the corner, by symmetry.
options.feedback: Symmetry is a tempting argument and it is wrong: the one-sided slopes are −1 and +1, and a limit with two answers has none.

explanationVariants: A corner (two one-sided slopes), a cusp (slopes running to ±∞ in opposite directions), a vertical tangent (slope infinite), and any discontinuity — all kill f′.
In every case the defining limit fails to produce one finite number.

widget.prompt: At which of these does f′ FAIL to exist?

items.label: A corner, like |x| at 0
items.feedback: Two one-sided slopes that disagree — the limit has no single value.

items.label: A jump discontinuity
items.feedback: If f is not even continuous, no tangent can exist. Differentiable ⇒ continuous, so not-continuous ⇒ not-differentiable.

items.label: A vertical tangent, like ∛x at 0
items.feedback: The slope runs off to infinity, and infinity is not a number. The tangent exists as a LINE but the derivative does not exist as a VALUE.

items.label: A smooth minimum, like x² at 0
items.feedback: Perfectly differentiable: f′(0) = 0. A flat tangent is still a tangent.

widget.missFeedback: Ask whether the limit [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h settles on ONE finite number.
widget.successFeedback: Corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities all break the limit. A flat tangent breaks nothing.

steps.body:
So "differentiable" is a stronger promise than "continuous": it says the curve is **locally straight**. Magnify a differentiable point far enough and the curve becomes indistinguishable from its tangent.

Magnify a corner and it stays a corner, forever. That is the honest test.
Now a point where the slope does exist.

widget.prompt: f(x) = x². Drag the point until the tangent's slope reads 2, and watch how closely the tangent line lies along the curve wherever you stop.
widget.successFeedback: Slope 2, at x = 1. Notice what held at every stop along the way: the tangent lay flat against the curve for a short stretch either side of the point. Nowhere on this curve did the line have to choose between two slopes.
widget.lowFeedback: The readout is under 2 here — the curve is either still tilting downward or climbing too gently. Drag to the right.
widget.highFeedback: The readout is over 2 here — the curve has already steepened past it. Drag back to the left.

explanationVariants: Zooming into a differentiable point flattens the curve onto its tangent — that is what having a derivative MEANS geometrically.
A corner survives every magnification, which is exactly why no tangent fits it.

widget.prompt: You magnify a graph at a point and it becomes indistinguishable from a straight line. What have you shown?

options.label: f is differentiable there — locally straight is what having a derivative looks like.
options.feedback: Right, and it is the geometric meaning of the limit: the closer you look, the better the tangent fits.

options.label: f is a straight line.
options.feedback: Only NEAR that point. Zoom back out and it may be a wild curve — local straightness is a local claim.

options.label: f′ = 0 there.
options.feedback: The line you see can have any slope. Locally straight says a tangent EXISTS, not that it is flat.

options.label: Nothing — every graph looks straight up close.
options.feedback: Not so: magnify |x| at its corner and it stays bent at exactly the same angle, no matter how far you zoom.

hints: Go through the list and ask, at each x: does the limit [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h give one finite number?
A jump kills it. A corner kills it. A vertical tangent kills it. A flat tangent does not.
There are three failures and one perfectly good derivative.
explanationVariants: The jump at x = −2, the corner at x = 0 and the vertical tangent at x = 3 all destroy the limit: three failures. The smooth minimum at x = 5 has f′ = 0, which is a perfectly good derivative.
A flat tangent is a tangent. An absent one is not.

widget.prompt: A function has a jump at x = −2, a corner at x = 0, a vertical tangent at x = 3, and a smooth minimum at x = 5. At how many of these four points does f′ FAIL to exist?

commonErrors.feedback: The smooth minimum is fine — a horizontal tangent is still a tangent, and f′ = 0 there. Only the first three break.
All three of the jump, the corner and the vertical tangent break the limit. Only the smooth minimum survives.
Each of the jump, the corner and the vertical tangent kills the limit in its own way — that is three failures.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Jump, corner and vertical tangent: three failures. The smooth minimum has f′ = 0, which exists.

steps.body: A derivative is a limit, and limits can fail.
takeaways: Differentiable ⇒ continuous. The converse is false, and |x| at 0 is the counterexample.
Corners, cusps, vertical tangents and discontinuities all destroy f′.
Differentiable means locally straight: zoom in far enough and the curve becomes its tangent.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: stop taking limits by hand. One rule handles every power at once.

concept.body: Ask the one question the definition asks: does [f(x+h) − f(x)]/h settle on a single finite number as h → 0? A corner gives two answers. A jump gives none. A vertical tangent gives infinity. Only a settled, finite value counts.

explanationVariants: Approaching the corner from the left gives −1 and from the right gives +1, so the limit has two answers and therefore none.
Two one-sided limits that disagree is exactly how a limit fails.

widget.prompt: At the corner of |x|, the left slope is −1 and the right slope is +1. Does f′(0) exist?

options.label: No — the two sides disagree, so the limit has no single value.
options.feedback: Right. A limit must settle on ONE number, and these two never meet.

options.label: Yes — it is the average, 0.
options.feedback: Averaging two disagreeing one-sided limits is not something the definition permits. When they disagree, the limit does not exist.
